nuggets.summary: Dan Price, CEO of the payment-processing company Gravity Payments, says he ranks three business priorities explicitly, in order: keep existing clients, do more for existing clients today than yesterday, and only then pursue new clients — with new-client acquisition deliberately kept a distant third priority. He argues most companies do the reverse, taking current clients and employees for granted while chasing the next new client or hire, which erodes the loyalty base that actually drives growth through referrals and retention. The non-obvious part is treating "new business" as the lowest, not highest, growth lever, on the theory that under-delivering to existing customers while chasing new ones is optimizing backwards.
nuggets.quote: Number one is keep your clients. Number two is do more for your clients today than you did yesterday. Have a better deal for them today than you did yesterday. And then number three is get new clients. And I try to make number three, like a distant priority and growth compared to one and two.

nuggets.summary: Price says he has settled on roughly 25% annual growth as the deliberate target rate for Gravity Payments — fast enough to feel challenging and exciting, but slow enough that the team can keep its priorities straight and maintain work-life balance over a multi-decade horizon. Counterintuitively, most of his energy as CEO goes toward moderating or slowing growth rather than accelerating it, even though the company has hit 100%-plus growth in some periods. This runs against the standard instinct to maximize growth at all costs; instead he treats growth as something to be matched to the company's spending and capacity, with sustainability as the actual constraint.
nuggets.quote: My theoretical belief is that for a business like ours, 25% is the right growth amount... this might surprise everybody here. Most of the time I'm spending more time and energy trying to slow down our growth rate as opposed to speed it up or at least moderate it.

nuggets.summary: Before taking any outside money, Price spent a night researching how venture capital actually works and became averse to one specific mechanic: preferred stock, which he saw as creating conflicts between founder and investor in any outcome short of a moon-shot exit. When he met with Madrona Venture Group's partners, he told them upfront he'd only accept the investment on common-stock terms; when a partner said their limited-partner agreement wouldn't allow that, he got up and left within five minutes. Years later, one of those same partners told him in an elevator, unprompted, that they should have done the deal anyway — an example of a founder isolating one specific deal term, not valuation or amount, as the real point of misalignment and treating it as non-negotiable.
nuggets.quote: I'm not going to do preferred stock. So if you're open to doing common stock, your valuation is fine. Your funding amount is fine... And if you want to do preferred stock, I won't do it... our limited partner agreement does not allow us to do that. And I literally, like within five minutes, got up and left.

nuggets.summary: Asked how to bootstrap instead of raising VC, Price lays out a concrete funding mechanism: do custom consulting or service work for a client, and in the best case, structure the engagement so the client pays for the development of a product you then own the IP to and can productize for other customers later. He adds that when you can afford it, doing this initial work for free rather than charging can be more valuable than the cash, because the real asset being built is the relationship, trust, and experience with a prototype customer. This reframes "consulting to bootstrap" from just a cash-flow survival tactic into a deliberate IP-ownership and go-to-market strategy.
nuggets.quote: the only way to build a product company is to do a service first, right?... you can find somebody who's willing to pay for all the development to have that customized where you then own the product and own the IP and can productize it out to other people... it's kind of good to not charge them.

nuggets.summary: Early in building his hiring process, Price noticed a high no-show rate for scheduled in-person interviews and built a cheap filter to catch it before it wasted his time: as soon as a resume looked decent, he'd immediately reply with a copy-pasted email interview rather than book a meeting slot. About half of the candidates who would have no-showed the in-person interview also failed to respond to the email version, meaning the email step surfaced the same low-commitment signal at near-zero cost. It's a generalizable pre-screen: add a low-friction, asynchronous step before spending real calendar time, and treat non-response as the same disqualifying signal a no-show would be.
nuggets.quote: I would set up a bunch of interviews and a bunch of people wouldn't show up. So I decided, okay, I'm going to get a resume. And then I'm going to immediately, if the resume is like any good at all, I'm going to reply and copy and paste an email interview. And the half of the people that wouldn't show up for the in-person interview also wouldn't respond to this email interview.

nuggets.summary: To make the value of unglamorous frontline work visible, Price uses a specific unit-economics exercise: he asked his team whether losing one client versus gaining five clients was roughly equivalent, and they were ambivalent — which by his math implied losing a single client actually costs the company about $150,000 against a client lifetime value of roughly $30,000, a five-times multiplier. The technique, not the specific figure, is the takeaway: translating an abstract "retention matters" message into a concrete number reframes what a low-wage employee's day-to-day work is actually worth to the business, which is a more durable motivator than pay alone.
nuggets.quote: One of my clients, I have a lifetime value just directly on that client of like 30 grand. And if I figure -- when I asked our team like do you think if we lose one client, would you rather lose one client or gain five? They were kind of ambivalent about the answer. That means that if we lose one client it costs $150,000.

nuggets.summary: Price says he personally makes very few decisions, because his operating belief is that people overrate "good judgment" as a decision-making skill and underrate how hard it is to simply perceive the underlying data accurately. His practice is to invest the group's energy into deeply understanding the actual situation first; once that's done thoroughly, the right choice is usually obvious, and often it isn't even a binary pick between two options but a third, hybrid path the group invents once it truly understands the data. This inverts the common leadership self-image of "I'm a good decision-maker" into "I'm good at making sure we understand reality first."
nuggets.quote: we way underestimate how difficult it is to accurately perceive the data that's in front of us. And we don't spend enough time and energy on that. We overestimate the importance of good judgment or good decision making... a lot of times it's not A or B. It's a C or it's some kind of hybrid or combination.

nuggets.summary: When Price was named Entrepreneur of the Year and his father heard the news, the reaction wasn't congratulations — his father called it "a character test," explaining that whatever character had been sufficient to be a baseline decent human being the day before was no longer sufficient now that Price had this platform. The framing is that the bar for "decent" isn't fixed; it rises in proportion to the influence, visibility, or opportunity a person is given, so gaining a platform is itself a demand for more character, not just a reward for past behavior. It's a useful reframe for anyone whose visibility or responsibility is expanding quickly: the standard you're held to moves with your reach, not your intentions.
nuggets.quote: whatever character was required of you yesterday is no longer sufficient today to be just a baseline like decent human being. So if you want to be a decent human being, the requisite character is now quite a bit higher.

nuggets.summary: When a client fraud incident wiped out roughly a third of the company's bank balance and left the risk-management team too shaken to focus, Price didn't open with a strategy session — he assigned each team member a character from the then-popular TV show House, played the lead role himself, and ran the problem-solving as a whiteboard session inside that frame; the team's mood visibly shifted and they recovered about half the fraud losses. He used a similar device after a damaging media profile, having the team whiteboard "what was actually bad about this" next to "what was actually good about it" instead of staying stuck in feeling misrepresented. The generalizable move: when a team is emotionally stuck after a real setback, a lightweight fictional or structural frame can unstick people faster than a direct pep talk aimed straight at the problem.
nuggets.quote: I assigned a personality from House. I let them pick for each person. And then I pretended I was House and we did a whiteboard session and you could see their eyes light up and all of a sudden we're solving the problem. We actually solved about half of the fraud that we're under.

nuggets.summary: In response to broader commoditization of creative and knowledge work, Gravity Payments started asking employees to literally sign work they produce — a blog post, a design, a paper, a photograph — even though the signer could later leave the company and the practice looks off-brand for consistent corporate output. The reasoning is that the act of signing tells the employee the work is treated as art rather than a disposable task, which shifts how they approach it: they start bringing an artistic-creator mindset instead of a task-completion mindset. It's a low-cost structural nudge — one small policy change — aimed at raising internal quality and ownership rather than a training program or incentive-pay scheme.
nuggets.quote: if you're going to write a paper or if you're going to write a blog post or if you're going to design something or if you're going to take a photograph, why don't you sign it?... now all of a sudden they have to take an artistic creators approach to that thing.

nuggets.summary: Gravity's CTO — a former First Data executive — flew round-trip same-day for a 20-minute coffee with Price after emailing his assistant out of the blue, then eventually joined the company at an 85% pay cut. Her motivation traced back 15 years: as an executive at First Data, she'd proposed that leadership give up bonuses to save jobs during layoffs and was laughed out of the room, and she'd carried that unresolved criticism ever since; she wanted to talk to someone else who'd faced similar mockery for a values-driven idea. The lesson Price draws is that being genuinely, publicly unconventional about your values doesn't just risk ridicule — it becomes a strong recruiting signal for the specific high-caliber people who share that value and have felt isolated for it, which no salary increase could replicate.
nuggets.quote: my CTO she took an 85% pay cut to work at Gravity... she said hey why don't we all give up our bonuses for the next two years. And we can save 12% of the jobs that we're cutting... She got laughed out of the room... she just wanted to talk to somebody else who had had some similar criticisms levied against them.

nuggets.summary: Price describes a trait he consciously chooses whether to work on each day: he cares so much about substance (getting the best outcome for someone) that he tends to disregard style entirely (how it's delivered, whether people find him likable), which he admits makes him difficult to work with for most people, since most people weight style over substance. He explicitly separates "wanting someone to succeed" from "wanting someone to like me or give me credit," treating the former as the actual job and the latter as optional. The useful reframe for any leader whose bluntness creates friction is naming which of the two — substance or style — is actually being optimized in a given interaction, since most workplace friction comes from a mismatch on that axis.
nuggets.quote: because I care so much about the substance, most of the time I completely disregard the style, which makes me incompatible to work with almost anybody... I don't care if somebody likes me that much... I care about that person being successful.

nuggets.summary: Price credits two peer organizations — EO (Entrepreneurs' Organization, which requires $1M+ revenue to join) and YPO — with keeping him grounded once he became a public figure, specifically because the CEOs in those groups don't care about his media profile, TV appearances, or magazine covers, and treat him as a peer regardless. The mechanism is deliberate: rather than seeking mentors impressed by his accomplishments, he seeks a peer network selected for indifference to status, which functions as a check against the ego inflation that public attention naturally produces. The actionable point is to evaluate a peer group by how little your accomplishments matter to how they treat you, not by how impressed they are with you.
nuggets.quote: having those people in my life through those organizations that don't care. They literally just don't care. You know, if I'm on The Daily Show or Inc. Magazine or something, they don't care. That's so positive.

nuggets.summary: Price frames his own skill development as a race against the job itself: given how fast his industry and company are changing, he says he can be 100% certain that his current skill set will be inadequate for his role in two years unless he actively outpaces the job's rising requirements — for some industries, he notes, that window could be as short as six months. This turns "keep learning" from generic advice into a specific, falsifiable claim: today's competence guarantees tomorrow's incompetence unless it's actively outrun, which is a useful test for judging whether your current skill-building pace actually matches your role's growth rate.
nuggets.quote: I can say with 100% certainty that two years from now, with the skills I have and the competence I have today, I'm going to be incompetent to do my job two years from now unless I outpace what the requirements are of the job.

nuggets.summary: Price pushes back on the popular narrative that industries are consolidating into fewer, larger players, arguing that in payments specifically the opposite is happening: more players — software companies, integrators, niche vertical providers — are working together seamlessly in a single transaction than ever before, largely by embedding payments directly into third-party software so the software company gets a supplemental revenue stream and the merchant gets a better-run business. He suspects this fragmentation-into-partnership pattern generalizes to other industries beyond payments. For anyone scouting opportunities in a market assumed to be consolidating, this is a concrete counter-signal: the more valuable entry point may be becoming an embedded partner inside many other companies' products rather than competing head-on as a standalone player.
nuggets.quote: as much as there's a lot of noise that would suggest there's tons of consolidation and there's fewer companies and more big companies kind of taking over the world. In my industry, it's exactly the opposite... there's more players working more seamlessly together in every transaction and every part of the business management process than there ever has been.

nuggets.summary: Gravity Payments' founding value proposition was framed as a specific ratio rather than a vague "better service" pitch: give merchants three times the service for one third of the cost. Price admits he didn't actually know whether that ratio was financially sustainable when he started — it worked out because the resulting referrals and client retention ended up high enough to make the economics work at scale, not because the math was proven up front. The takeaway is that an extreme, quantified value-asymmetry promise (3x service at 1/3 cost, not just "better and cheaper") can be a viable go-to-market bet without a proven model, if it's strong enough to generate compounding referral and retention effects that offset thinner unit margins.
nuggets.quote: we want to give so much value, you know, try to go 10x value for our merchants. We want to give them three times the service for one third the cost. That was the initial idea of the business. I wasn't smart enough to know if it could be financially viable, but we ended up with so many referrals and such high client retention that it ended up kind of working out.

nuggets.summary: Responding to a photographer's observation that image and creative work has been commoditized by free or cheap supply, Price says he sees the same forces in his own commoditized payments industry, but reports feeling less pricing pressure now than in the past — because the industry itself is starting to recognize that "the real commodity is trust," not the base service. His read is that low-cost commoditization runs in a pendulum: once a market pushes hard enough on low cost, buyers (even ones near the bottom of the economic ladder) start valuing and paying for quality, artistry, and trustworthiness again, rather than trust and commoditization being permanently opposed forces. This is a useful counter-frame for anyone assuming a market's race-to-the-bottom on price is a one-way, permanent trend rather than a swing that reverses.
nuggets.quote: I feel less pricing pressure today in some ways than I ever have in an industry where it's getting more commoditized every day because people in my industry, people are starting to say, well, the real commodity is trust.
